Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Pendleton OR
949 PM PST Fri Nov 20 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...
- Showers and mountain snow Saturday. 

- Widespread showers and mountain snow Tuesday through Thursday. 

- Breezy winds Tuesday and Wednesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Current radar and visible satellite imagery shows light returns
moving into the Columbia Basin from the north under partly 
cloudy to mostly cloudy skies. This is in response to an upper 
level trough dropping south through Alberta as a transient upper
level ridge moves onshore. The incoming ridge will attribute to
the development of overnight and Saturday morning fog over much
of the region, especially across the Columbia Basin/Gorge, Blue
Mountain foothills, and the Yakima/Kittitas Valleys. Overnight 
and morning temperatures are also expected to be below 
freezing, so travel concerns in these areas will be compounded 
as freezing fog may lead to slick roadways and sidewalks. Use 
caution if traveling during the morning hours, and make sure to
check road conditions and the forecast for any issued 
fog/freezing fog advisories. Conditions should improve by around
noon, but some stubborn areas of the Yakima and Kittitas 
Valleys may linger into the afternoon. 

The upper level ridge continues to pass through the region as 
an incoming upper level low pressure approaches the coast
Saturday. A pressure gradient will develop along this boundary 
between the departing high pressure and incoming low pressure, 
attributing to breezy winds across portions of Central and 
Eastern Oregon - especially across the Grande Ronde Valley. GFS 
guidance suggests a 3-4 mb pressure gradient between Baker City
and Meacham Saturday afternoon, which correlates to south winds
of 15-25 mph with gusts around 35 mph. The arrival of these 
winds will coincide with showers beginning across the Cascades. 
Snow levels will start out at 2500-3500 feet Saturday afternoon,
dropping to 1500-2500 feet by Sunday morning. Minimal moisture 
is associate with this system as the fetch is quite short and 
continental in origin, leading to lower elevation rain amounts 
of less than 0.04" and mountain snowfall of around an inch at 
most. Precipitation chances will peak between 4 PM Saturday 
(Central Oregon/Cascades) and 4 AM Sunday (Columbia Basin/Blue 
Mountains). These conditions are associated with a shortwave 
passing through the area as the parent low pressure system stays
offshore and lifts north, dissipating along the British 
Columbia coast as another transient ridge of high pressure 
builds along the coast. 

Much like the weekend system, this ridge of high pressure will
be followed closely by a stronger, more robust system that 
nears the coast early Tuesday. Snow levels are expected to 
slowly rise from around 3000 feet Tuesday morning to near 5000 
feet by the afternoon. There will be about +/-500 feet gradient 
north to south, so the Washington Cascade Passes are currently 
expected to receive 3-5 inches of snow at pass level, with a 
range of 1-3 inches of snow across the Oregon Cascade Passes. 
Confidence in these amounts is moderate (40-60%) as 21% of 
ensemble members align with the current forecast, with 49% 
suggesting a slightly drier outcome, and 30% of members 
advertising an outcome of more snowfall. These difference 
average +/- 2-3 inches at Washington Cascade Pass level in 
relation to the current forecast, and are a direct result of
guidance struggling with the overall strength of the incoming
system. This will be further analyzed as the event nears, as 
some of these outcomes approach or exceed advisory snowfall 
amounts. However, advisory-level snowfall is quite low (10%) at
this time. Widespread rainfall is expected across lower 
elevations, with amounts between 0.10-0.20" Tuesday through 
Wednesday. 

Also similar to the weekend system, wind concerns will again
arise. Breezy winds are expected across much of the region, 
especially over the same areas of Central Oregon and the Grande
Ronde Valley. The base of the Blue Mountain foothills will also
experience elevated winds, with downslope wind potential 
extending from early morning Tuesday to Wednesday afternoon. 
Wind products are much more likely with this event as the GFS 
highlights a 6-7 mb pressure gradient between Ontario and 
Meacham and between Baker City and Meacham. The projected peak 
of the pressure gradient is expected both Tuesday and Wednesday 
mornings. The NBM advertises a 60-65% chance of advisory level 
wind gusts (+45 mph) across the Grande Ronde Valley Tuesday and 
a 40-50% chance on Wednesday, but only a 10% chance of high wind
warning criteria being reached (+58 mph gusts) either day. 
Thus, south winds of 25-35 mph with gusts of 40-50 mph are 
expected early Tuesday morning through Wednesday morning. 75

.AVIATION /06Z TAFS THROUGH 06Z SUNDAY/...
VFR conditions present for all TAF sites except KPSC. Going from 06Z 
to the morning period shows fog developing for Pasco with lowering 
cloud bases, mixing near the surface producing 1/2 mile visibility 
fog at the highest impact. Confidence of fog below 1/2 mile is 
moderate to high (50-70%) and should clear up into midday around 18z 
onward. Additionally, KALW and KYKM have low confidence (~30%) of 
fog and low stratus. If fog and low stratus would generate for KALW, 
it would have similar timing to KPSC. While KYKM is uncertain of 
when it would start and stop as conditions are favorable for fog 
currently.
